of patients who experienced nausea or vomiting.271 Other publications 
have also cited the value of palonosetron for patients receiving multiday 
anticancer therapy.275,276 Further studies are needed to define whether a 
need exists for repeat dosing of palonosetron in the setting of multiday 
anticancer therapy. 

5-HT3 Antagonists 
For multiday anticancer regimens, a 5-HT3 antagonist should be 
administered each day before the first dose of MEC or HEC. IV 
palonosetron, subcutaneous granisetron, or transdermal granisetron may 
be used before the start of a 3-day anticancer regimen instead of multiple 
daily doses of PO/IV 5-HT3 antagonists.271,272 It is not known whether 
repeat dosing with subcutaneous granisetron for multiday regimens would 
be effective. Repeat dosing of palonosetron (0.25 mg IV) is likely to be 
safe, based on the dose-ranging phase 2 trial and the three phase 3 trials 
using palonosetron as a single fixed dose (0.75 mg IV).68,70,71,273 Compared 
to the approved dose of palonosetron of 0.25 mg IV, these higher doses 
were not associated with significantly different adverse events. 

NK1 RAs 
The potential role of NK1 RAs in the antiemetic management of multiday 
anticancer therapy has been investigated in several studies.148,236,277-279 In a 
randomized phase 3 trial, the efficacy of adding PO aprepitant (vs. 
placebo) to an antiemetic regimen with a 5-HT3 antagonist and 
dexamethasone was evaluated in patients with germ cell cancers 
undergoing two cycles of a 5-day cisplatin combination therapy regimen (n 
= 69 evaluable).277 Patients were randomized to receive PO aprepitant 
(125 mg PO day 3, 80 mg days 4–7) or placebo, combined with a 5-HT3 
antagonist (days 1–5) and dexamethasone (20 mg days 1–2) during the 
first cycle, and then crossed over to the opposite antiemetic regimen 
during the second cycle of anticancer therapy. Thus, patients served as 
their own controls after receiving either PO aprepitant or placebo for cycle 
1. Palonosetron was excluded from the options for 5-HT3 antagonists due 
to its longer half-life.277 The primary endpoint of the study was CR (no 
emetic episodes and no rescue medication) during the overall study period 
(days 1–8). The CR rate for the overall study period was significantly 
higher with PO aprepitant compared with placebo (42% vs. 13%; P < 
.001). The CR rates were also higher with PO aprepitant during the acute 
phase (days 1–5; 47% vs. 15%; P < .001) and delayed phase (days 6–8; 
63% vs. 35%; P < .001).277 No statistically significant differences were 
observed between treatment regimens in terms of nausea (based on 
patient-reported VAS). Importantly, no increase in toxicity with PO 
aprepitant compared with placebo was reported.277 

The optimal dosing with palonosetron, either daily or less frequently, in the 
setting of multiday anticancer regimens is not yet known. In one study, 
patients receiving highly emetogenic multiday cisplatin-based therapy for 
testicular cancer (N = 41) received multiday dosing of palonosetron (0.25 
mg IV on days 1, 3, and 5) and dexamethasone, which prevented nausea 
and emesis in most patients on days 1 to 5 (51%) and on days 6 to 9 
(83%); the most common adverse events were mild headache and 
constipation.274 A study assessed palonosetron given for 1, 2, or 3 days in 
combination with dexamethasone for patients receiving multiday high-dose 
anticancer regimens prior to HCT for multiple myeloma (N = 73); during 
the 7-day emesis prevention period, approximately 40% to 45% of patients 
had no emesis (with no differences observed between palonosetron 
treatment groups), and no serious adverse events were reported. 
However, even among the patients who received either 2 or 3 days of 
palonosetron, only 20% had a CR (ie, emesis free without rescue 
medication).119 Another study found that a palonosetron/dexamethasone 
regimen appeared to be more effective for multiday anticancer therapy 
than an ondansetron/dexamethasone regimen; patients received a second 
dose of palonosetron for breakthrough emesis, which was effective in 67%

an average of 10.6 (standard deviation [SD], 0.95) emesis-free days over 
an 11-day observation period, and few 1–2 grade adverse events (eg, 
headache, nausea, diarrhea). These findings are consistent with an Italian 
phase 2a multicenter study on NEPA without dexamethasone in patients 
with relapsed/refractory aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma (N = 70).282 
This study reported an overall CR value of 87.1% and complete control 
percentage of 85.7%. Less than 10% of patients experienced moderate or 
severe episodes of nausea and only one adverse event was reported 
(constipation). 

The addition of PO aprepitant to granisetron and dexamethasone was 
evaluated in patients receiving multiday HEC and MEC (N = 78). In this 
study, the three-drug antiemetic regimen was given during anticancer 
therapy; PO aprepitant and dexamethasone were given for an additional 2 
days following anticancer therapy.279 A CR (during the time period from 
day 1 until 5 days after anticancer therapy) was observed in 58% and 73% 
of patients who received antiemetic regimens for HEC and MEC, 
respectively.279 In a multicenter phase 2 study, an extended 7-day regimen 
with PO aprepitant (125 mg PO day 1, 80 mg days 2–7) combined with a 
5-HT3 antagonist (days 1–5) and dexamethasone (8 mg PO days 1–8) 
was evaluated in patients with germ cell tumors undergoing anticancer 
therapy cycles with 5-day cisplatin-based regimens (N = 50).278 During 
cycle 1 of anticancer therapy, 96% of patients had no emesis on day 1 and 
82% had no emesis during days 1 to 7. In addition, 71% had no nausea on 
day 1 of cycle 1, and 27% had no nausea during days 1 to 7. More than 
80% of patients had no emesis on any given day of any given anticancer 
therapy cycle. No unexpected or serious adverse events were reported.278 
In another study, aprepitant (125 mg day 1, 80 mg days 2–5) combined 
with palonosetron (0.75 mg day 1) and dexamethasone (9.9 mg day 1, 6.6 
mg days 2–8) was evaluated in 30 patients with testicular germ cell tumors 
receiving 5-day cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy. Ninety percent 
of the patients achieved CR in the first round of chemotherapy; 82% and 
78% also achieved CR in the second and third rounds of chemotherapy.280 

An open-label, randomized controlled study compared the efficacy and 
safety of fosaprepitant (150 mg) given on days 1 to 3 (prolonged group) 
versus on day 1 (regular group) in patients receiving HECs.283 Patients 
were randomly assigned to the prolonged group (N = 77) and regular 
group (N = 79). In the prolonged versus regular group, a statistically 
significant lower incidence of nausea (6.17% vs. 12.66%, P = .0056) and 
slightly lower incidence of grade 1 vomiting (1.62% vs. 3.80%, P = .0953) 
in the delayed phase was seen. This study concluded that prolonged use 
of fosaprepitant was safe and that the two groups did not have significant 
differences in adverse events within the delayed phase. NK1 antagonists 
may be used for multiday anticancer therapy likely to be moderately or 
highly emetogenic and associated with significant risk for delayed nausea 
and emesis. As per the labeled indication, 125 mg of PO aprepitant should 
be administered 1 hour prior to anticancer therapy on day 1, along with a 
5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone. Aprepitant 80 mg PO should be 
administered daily on days 2 to 3 after the start of anticancer therapy 
along with dexamethasone.263 Repeated dosing of PO aprepitant over 
multiple cycles of cisplatin-based therapy appears to be feasible and well 
tolerated. Importantly, protection from emesis and from significant nausea 
was maintained during the subsequent cycles of emetogenic anticancer 
therapy.263,277 Based on smaller studies, aprepitant 80 mg PO may be 
safely administered beyond day 3 of initiating anticancer therapy.133,278 

Multiday dosing of netupitant/palonosetron fixed combination in 
association with BEAM (carmustine, etoposide, cytarabine, and 
melphalan)/FEAM (fotemustine, etoposide, cytarabine, and melphalan) 
prior to HCT was evaluated in two phase 2 studies. In a single-center, 
single-arm, phase 2 study investigating the efficacy and safety of NEPA 
and dexamethasone for the prevention of CINV in patients receiving 
BEAM therapy prior to HCT (N = 43), this antiemetic combination was 
deemed safe and effective.281 A CR was achieved in 3 patients (30%) with

Alternatively, for HEC regimens, aprepitant injectable emulsion 130 mg IV 
or fosaprepitant 150 mg IV with dexamethasone may be given on day 1, 
with no need for PO aprepitant on days 2 to 3, with recommended dosing 
of dexamethasone on days 2 to 4. Data are not available for repeat dosing 
of aprepitant injectable emulsion, or PO rolapitant. 

Atypical Antipsychotics 
If olanzapine is being used prophylactically as part of the antiemetic 
regimen, the Panel recommends that it may be used once daily (prior to 
chemotherapy or at bedtime) and continued for 2 to 3 days after 
chemotherapy for regimens that are likely to cause significant delayed 
emesis.284 

Summary 

The NCCN Guidelines for Antiemesis provide an overview of the principles 
for preventing or substantially decreasing anticancer agent–induced or 
RT-induced nausea and/or vomiting and provide recommendations for 
prophylactic antiemetic regimens based on the emetogenic potential of 
anticancer agents. Prophylactic antiemetic regimens are recommended for 
patients who will receive emetogenic anticancer agents, because it is 
harder to control nausea and/or vomiting once it has started. Although 
vomiting can often be prevented or substantially decreased by using 
prophylactic antiemetic regimens, nausea is harder to control. This 
Discussion text for antiemesis describes these updates in greater detail, in 
particular the clinical trial data and references that support the NCCN 
Panel’s recommendations in the algorithm.

Patients need to be protected throughout the full period of risk. • Oral (PO) and parenteral serotonin receptor antagonists (5-HT3 RAs) have equivalent efficacy when used at the appropriate doses and intervals. • Consider the toxicity of the specific antiemetic(s). See Pharmacologic Considerations for Antiemetic Prescribing (AE-B). • Choice of antiemetic(s) used should be based on the emetic risk of the therapy, prior experience with antiemetics, and patient factors. Continuous infusion may make an agent less emetogenic. nodes.text: • For uses of antiemetics for nausea/vomiting that are not related to radiation and/or anticancer therapy, see NCCN Guidelines for Palliative Care. • For multi-drug regimens, select antiemetic therapy based on the drug with the highest emetic risk. See Adult Parenteral Anticancer Agents – Emetogenic Potential (AE-3 through AE-5), and see Adult Oral Anticancer Agents – Emetogenic Potential (AE-9). • Antiemetic regimens added to a patient's anticancer agents may have a potential risk for drug-drug interactions. However, no clinically significant drug- drug interactions have emerged to date in randomized clinical trials of anticancer agents with antiemetics. The Panel feels, given a short duration of use (<4 days; not chronic use) of these prophylactic antiemetic regimens, they would not result in clinically relevant interactions with anticancer agents. However, in all situations where medications are prescribed, clinicians must balance the benefits and risks for each patient. • Consider using an H2 blocker or proton pump inhibitor (PPI) to prevent dyspepsia, which can mimic nausea. • Lifestyle measures may help to alleviate nausea/vomiting, such as eating small frequent meals, choosing healthful foods, controlling the amount of food consumed, and eating food at room temperature. A dietary consult may also be useful. See NCI’s “Eating Hints: Before, During, and After Cancer Treatment” (https://www.cancer.gov/publications/patient-education/eating-hints). • While anticancer agents or RT-induced nausea and vomiting can significantly impact a patient's quality of life and lead to poor outcomes, providers must be aware of the potential for the overuse of prophylactic antiemetics, especially for anticancer therapy with minimal and low emetic risks, which may expose the patient to potential adverse effects from antiemetic drugs and pose an undue economic burden. Guideline adherence is always encouraged. • When planning an antiemetic regimen, the health literacy of the patient must be considered, taking into account sociocultural differences. Effective provider-patient communication may improve patient satisfaction, adherence, safety, and outcomes. Clinicians need to identify language and literacy barriers and provide appropriate resources (eg, printed material, medication calendars, interpreter services) to help whenever possible. • The Panel acknowledges that many patients are interested in complementary and alternative medicines (CAM) to treat their cancer or cancer treatment-related side effects. To date, however, there are no high-level, large, randomized clinical trials demonstrating superior benefit for these types of therapies in place of conventional antiemetic drug therapy as recommended in this guideline for the prevention or treatment of CINV in adult patients. Patients who wish to supplement their conventional antiemetic therapy with CAM should consult their provider or pharmacist to ensure safety and appropriateness. • The Panel recognizes that high-dose chemotherapy in the setting of hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) is a unique and challenging situation where patients often have multiple risk factors for CINV in addition to intensive chemotherapy. As the majority of conditioning regimens used in the HCT setting are highly emetogenic, the Panel would encourage clinicians to refer to AE-6 as a basis for developing a personalized plan for CINV prevention. • The Panel is aware of the emerging clinical controversy that dexamethasone, with its broad immunosuppressive effect, could blunt the effect of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). To date, there are no randomized clinical trials that demonstrate the detriment of using dexamethasone as a prophylactic antiemetic when ICIs are used in combination with chemotherapy. The Panel recognizes some recent clinical trials that have not allowed dexamethasone when used solely as an antiemetic, and other publications that suggest a negative impact on outcomes when steroids are used with ICIs. Clinicians may wish to consider a dexamethasone-sparing approach (AE-B 2 of 6), or use alternative antiemetic agents, such as olanzapine for the purposes of delayed CINV prophylaxis, until more definitive data become available.

footnotes.text: Antiemetic regimens should be chosen based on the drug with the highest emetic risk as well as patient-specific risk factors.
Principles of Managing Multiday Emetogenic Chemotherapy Regimens (AE-A).
Pharmacologic Considerations for Antiemetic Prescribing (AE-B).

Data suggest that a 2.5-mg dose of olanzapine may be efficacious, especially when used as part of a 4-drug regimen. Olanzapine doses of 2.5–5 mg may be less effective than 10 mg when used as part of a 3-drug regimen. Consider lower doses, especially for patients who are older or who are at high risk for oversedation. Hashimoto H, et al. Lancet Oncol 2020;21:242-249; Bajpai J, et al. Lancet Oncol 2024;25:246-254. See Pharmacologic Considerations for Antiemetic Prescribing (AE- B).

nodes.text: RESPONSE

The general principle of breakthrough treatment is to add one agent from a different drug class to the current regimen. • Atypical antipsychotic: Olanzapine 2.5–10 mg PO daily (bedtime) (category 1, preferred) • Cannabinoid: Dronabinol capsules 5–10 mg, or dronabinol PO solution 2.1–4.2 mg/m², PO 3–4 times daily • Anticholinergics: Scopolamine 1.5 mg transdermal patch 1 patch every 72 h • Dopamine-receptor antagonists: Haloperidol 0.5–2 mg PO/IV every 4–6 h Metoclopramide 10–20 mg PO/IV every 4–6 h Phenothiazine: ◊Prochlorperazine 25 mg suppository (supp) PR every 12 h or 10 mg PO/IV every 6 h ◊Promethazine 25 mg supp PR every 6 h or 12.5–25 mg PO every 4–6 h • 5-HT3 RA: Granisetron 1–2 mg PO daily or 1 mg PO twice a day (BID) or 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 1 mg) IV daily or 3.1 mg/24-h transdermal patch every 7 days Ondansetron 8 mg PO/IV every 8–12 h (16–24 mg total daily dose) • Corticosteroid: Dexamethasone 4–8 mg PO/IV daily • Benzodiazepine: Lorazepam 0.5–1 mg PO/sublingual (SL)/IV every 6 h

footnotes.text: Pharmacologic Considerations for Antiemetic Prescribing (AE-B).

Use of corticosteroid premedications should be avoided with cellular therapies. Clinicians may wish to consider a dexamethasone-sparing approach with ICI therapy as well. See Pharmacologic Considerations for Antiemetic Prescribing (AE-B).
Dronabinol PO solution has greater PO bioavailability than dronabinol capsules; 2.1 mg PO solution = 2.5 mg capsules.

While no clinically significant drug-drug interactions with short-term use of antiemetics have emerged to date in randomized clinical trials, the Panel would discourage combining multiple dopamine-receptor antagonists as this could increase the risk of extrapyramidal reactions. When used for breakthrough CINV, a single drug from this class could be utilized.

Especially for patients where anxiety may be contributing to breakthrough CINV. See Principles of Emesis Control for the Patient with Cancer (AE-1) and Pharmacologic Considerations for Antiemetic Prescribing (AE-B).

When combined with IV agents in a combination anticancer therapy regimen, the antiemetic recommendations for the agent with the highest level of emetogenicity should be followed. nodes.text: Breakthrough Treatment required (PEDAE-12)
Continue PRN dosing
Breakthrough Treatment not required
SUBSEQUENT CYCLES
BREAKTHROUGH TREATMENT FOR PEDIATRIC ANTICANCER THERAPY-INDUCED NAUSEA/VOMITING
RESPONSE

The general principle of breakthrough treatment is to add one agent from a different drug class to the current regimen. • Atypical antipsychotic: Olanzapine 0.05–0.2 mg/kg (2.5–10 mg) PO daily (bedtime) • Cannabinoid: Dronabinol 2.5–10 mg PO every 6–8 hours • Anticholinergics: Scopolamine 1.5 mg transdermal patch 0.5–1 patch every 72 hours • Dopamine-receptor antagonists: Metoclopramide 0.1–0.25 mg/kg PO/IV every 6 hours (max 10 mg/dose) Phenothiazine: ◊Prochlorperazine 0.1 mg/kg PO/IV every 6 hours (max 10 mg/dose) ◊Promethazine 0.25–0.5 mg/kg (6.25–25 mg/dose) PO/IV every 6 hours (only for patients ≥2 years of age) • 5-HT3 RA: Granisetron 0.01–0.04 mg/kg IV once or 0.04 mg/kg PO every 12–24 hours (max 2 mg/day) Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg or 5 mg/m (max 16 mg/dose or 0.45 mg/kg/day) PO/IV every 8–24 hours, not to exceed 3 doses/day (max 24 mg/day) • Corticosteroid: Dexamethasone PO/IV every 12–24 hours • Benzodiazepine: Lorazepam 0.025–0.05 mg/kg/dose PO/IV every 6 hours (max 2 mg/dose)

footnotes.text: Use of corticosteroid premedications should be avoided with cellular therapies. Clinicians may wish to consider a dexamethasone-sparing approach with ICI therapy as well. See Pharmacologic Considerations for Antiemetic Prescribing (AE-B).

No optimal pediatric dexamethasone dose has been identified. Dexamethasone doses may be individualized. Consider doses of 5–10 mg/m/day once daily or divided. Dexamethasone should be reduced by 50% when given concomitantly with NK1 RAs.
When not used as part of the acute and delayed emesis prevention regimen.
Dronabinol PO solution has greater PO bioavailability than dronabinol capsules; 2.1 mg PO solution = 2.5 mg capsules.
Do not cut patches. If 1/2 patch is needed, remove only 1/2 of the backing prior to application. Cover with occlusive dressing to keep in place.

While no clinically significant drug-drug interactions with short-term use of antiemetics have emerged to date in randomized clinical trials, the Panel would discourage combining multiple dopamine- receptor antagonists as this could increase the risk of extrapyramidal reactions. When used for breakthrough CINV, a single drug from this class could be utilized.
Especially for patients where anxiety may be contributing to breakthrough CINV.

nodes.text: Anticancer therapy and RT (including TBI)
PEDIATRIC ANTICIPATORY EMESIS – PREVENTION/TREATMENT

• Prevention is key: Use optimal antiemetic therapy during every cycle of treatment Avoid strong smells that may precipitate symptoms • Behavioral therapy: Relaxation/systematic desensitization Hypnosis Relaxation exercises ◊Guided imagery ◊PMR ◊Biofeedback ◊Music therapy Cognitive distraction Yoga (if approved by physician) • Acupuncture/acupressure • Consider anxiolytic therapy: Lorazepam 0.025–0.05 mg/kg/dose PO beginning on the night before treatment and then repeated the next day and/ or continued PO/IV every 6 hours before anticancer therapy begins (max 2 mg/dose) or Olanzapine 0.05–0.2 mg/kg (2.5–10 mg) PO once at bedtime prior to first dose of anticancer therapy

patient_population.definition: Whether the patient is managed on the adult or the pediatric pathway, as stated in the case description.

age_months.definition: Patient age in months as stated in the case description (3 years is 36 months).

anticancer_agent_route.definition: Class or route of the anticancer agent given in the case: parenteral, oral, radiopharmaceutical, none if no anticancer agent is given, or other.

agent_emesis_frequency_percent.definition: Frequency of emesis (percent of patients) documented for the anticancer agent or regimen in the case description.

radiation_regimen.definition: Radiation therapy described in the case: RT to the upper abdomen or localized sites, total body irradiation (TBI), anticancer therapy together with RT (including TBI), or other.

presenting_symptom.definition: Nausea and vomiting situation stated in the case: none, any nausea and/or vomiting, radiation-induced nausea/vomiting, or anticipatory nausea/vomiting.

nausea_vomiting_control.definition: Whether the patient's nausea and/or vomiting is controlled or uncontrolled at the time of assessment.

nausea_vomiting_timing.definition: Phase of nausea and/or vomiting stated in the case: acute (within 24 hours) or delayed (more than 24 hours after anticancer agent or RT), or other.

breakthrough_treatment_required.definition: Clinician judgement: a breakthrough (as-needed) antiemetic treatment is required for this patient.

breakthrough_treatment_frequently_requir.definition: Clinician judgement: breakthrough antiemetic treatment is frequently required for this patient.

able_to_receive_nk1_ra.criteria: able to receive an NK1 RA
able_to_receive_nk1_ra.definition: Clinician judgement: the patient is able to receive a neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist (NK1 RA).

able_to_receive_dexamethasone.definition: Clinician judgement: the patient is able to receive dexamethasone.

multidrug_regimen.definition: The anticancer treatment is a multi-drug regimen, as stated in the case description.

hct_conditioning_regimen.definition: The anticancer treatment is a hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) conditioning regimen, as stated in the case description.

patient_wishes_cam_supplement.definition: The patient wishes to supplement conventional antiemetic therapy with complementary and alternative medicine (CAM).

language_or_literacy_barrier.definition: The patient has a language or literacy barrier that affects understanding of antiemetic instructions.

guideline_section.definition: Which disease or subtype section of this guideline the case belongs to: the disease named in the guideline's page headings that the patient has (e.g. the tumor type or subtype).

pediatric_age_band.definition: Age band computed from age_months using the cut-offs printed in the pediatric boxes: 6 months and 3 years (36 months).

emetic_risk_category.definition: Adult emetic risk category computed from agent_emesis_frequency_percent. Oral agents: 30 percent or more is moderate to high, 10 to under 30 percent is low, under 10 percent is minimal. Parenteral, radiopharmaceutical and other agents: over 90 percent is high (AE-3 '>90%'), over 30 up to 90 percent is moderate (AE-3 '>30%-90%'), 10 up to and including 30 percent is low (AE-4 '10%-30%'), under 10 percent is minimal (AE-5 '<10%'). Categories 'minimal to low' and 'low and minimal' in the boxes are the union of low and minimal. Box ranges that name several categories (e.g. 'moderate to high') are encoded as an 'in' predicate over these values.

pediatric_emetic_risk_category.definition: Pediatric emetic risk category computed from agent_emesis_frequency_percent using the pediatric box ranges: moderate is over 30 percent to 90 percent, low is 10 percent to 30 percent inclusive, minimal is under 10 percent (the boxes' 'minimal to low' is under 30 percent, the union of low and minimal). Over 90 percent is high, matching the adult high threshold. Exactly 30 percent is low, not moderate. Box ranges that name several categories (e.g. 'moderate to high') are encoded as an 'in' predicate over these values.

notes.predicates: Conditions were drafted and reviewed by a language model (model_reviewed), not by clinicians. 'rejected' means the review rejected the draft; the box then needs clinician judgement. 'section_only' means the box only requires the patient to be in the page's guideline section.
